name: The doctrine of the 'idols' (bad habits of mind)
plain_explanation: Bacon identified recurring bad mental habits that lead people into error: idols of the tribe (biases built into human nature, like expecting more order in nature than exists), idols of the cave (an individual thinker's personal prejudices), idols of the market-place (being misled by the imprecision and tyranny of words), idols of the theatre (uncritical acceptance of received systems of thought, especially Aristotle and scholasticism), and idols of the schools (letting a rigid rule, like the syllogism, substitute for actual judgment).
precise_definition: Bacon's five 'idols,' as summarized by Russell: idols of the tribe are inherent in human nature (notably the habit of expecting more order in phenomena than actually exists); idols of the cave are personal prejudices of the individual investigator; idols of the market-place concern the tyranny of words and the difficulty of escaping their influence over thought; idols of the theatre concern uncritical acceptance of received systems of thought (chiefly Aristotle and the scholastics); idols of the schools consist in letting a blind rule (such as the syllogism) substitute for judgement in investigation.
why_it_mattered: This remains, per Russell, 'one of the most famous parts of Bacon's philosophy,' offering an enduring taxonomy of the sources of intellectual error that goes beyond simple logical fallacy to include psychological, social, and institutional causes of mistaken belief.
historical_origin: Bacon's own systematic classification, presented as part of his broader project of reforming scientific method.
examples: Idols of the tribe: expecting more order in nature than is actually present
Idols of the theatre: uncritical deference to Aristotle and scholasticism
